performers: The Mannes-Gimpel-Silva Trio: Leopold Mannes, piano; Bronislav Gimpel, violin; Luigi Silva, cello
intro: The third movement of the Piano Trio in G minor, Op. 17, is an Andante in G major in which the piano plays the melody alone before the violin and cello take it in turn. An agitated middle section interrupts, and when the opening returns, the cello has the tune over piano arpeggios.

sections.label: A · Piano, then violin and cello
A′ · Cello melody over piano arpeggios
sections.mNote: The violin plays pizzicato beneath the cello melody.

cues.title: Opening theme, piano alone
cues.text: The piano plays an eight-bar melody in G major alone, in six-eight time. From bar 9 the violin takes the melody over a pizzicato cello accompaniment. The cello takes the melody from bar 17.
cues.evidence: Clara Schumann, Piano Trio, first edition (Breitkopf & Härtel, plate 7562), printed p. 20: Andante, piano alone in bars 1–8, violin melody and pizzicato cello from bar 9, cello melody from bar 17. Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=4511&itemFileId=6784
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition of the Trio, 1846
cues.text: Clara wrote the Trio between May and September 1846. It was her first chamber composition, and she came to it after years of playing the chamber music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven at the piano.
cues.evidence: Robert Greenberg, Library of Congress National Recording Registry essay, p. 4, gives May–September 1846 and identifies the Trio as Clara’s first chamber composition, following her study and performance of Classical chamber works. https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/SchumannPianoTrios.pdf

cues.title: Middle section, più animato
cues.text: Più animato — more animated. From bar 25, rapid figures break up the strings’ long phrases, and the piano plays forte chords. This contrasting middle section of the Andante is in E minor.
cues.evidence: First edition, printed pp. 21–22: più animato at bar 25, forte piano chords and rapid string figures. The LA Phil programme note describes the Andante’s contrasting E-minor middle section: https://www.laphil.com/works/piano-trio
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening melody, cello
cues.text: At bar 53 the opening tempo and G major melody return, now in the cello rather than the piano, which first played it. The violin plays pizzicato. The piano plays broad arpeggios rising from the bass.
cues.evidence: First edition, printed p. 22, Tempo I at bar 53: cello melody, pizzicato violin and piano arpeggios; continuation on p. 23. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=4511&itemFileId=6784
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Decca recording, Mannes, Gimpel, Silva
cues.text: Leopold Mannes played the piano, Bronislav Gimpel the violin and Luigi Silva the cello. Their Decca LP coupled Clara’s Trio with a short B♭ major trio by Beethoven.
cues.evidence: Decca DL 9555, original side labels: named players, Clara’s Op. 17 and Beethoven’s posthumous B♭-major Trio. The coupling is also reviewed in Audio Engineering, September 1952, p. 48: https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Audio/Archive-Audio/50s/Audio-1952-09.pdf

composer.epithet: Performer on the concert platform for forty years, who wrote of making music, “It is the air I breathe.”
facts: Piano with her father Friedrich Wieck; private lessons in composition and languages
Leipzig début, 1828; last public concert, Frankfurt, 1891
A piano concerto, a piano trio, songs, romances and variations
composer.background:
On 9 November 1835 the sixteen-year-old Clara Wieck played her A minor Piano Concerto at the Leipzig Gewandhaus, with Mendelssohn conducting. In the middle movement the orchestra stops. The piano begins a Romance in A♭ major, and a solo cello joins it, so that for a few minutes the concerto is a duet. That evening Clara also played Mendelssohn’s Capriccio brillant, and with him and Louis Rakemann she played Bach’s Concerto for Three Keyboards.

She was born in Leipzig on 13 September 1819. Her mother, Mariane, was a pianist and singer; her father, Friedrich Wieck, taught piano and sold instruments. After their divorce in 1825, Clara remained with him. He arranged lessons in harmony, counterpoint and languages, supervised her practising and required daily walks. Private teachers supplied most of her education. He also managed her concert tours.
